items.title: What young adults with persistent musculoskeletal pain need from generative AI between visits
items.abstract: Abstract Patients increasingly consult generative AI, but how answers become action between visits is unclear. We interviewed 25 young adults in China with persistent, mainly musculoskeletal pain (17 used AI chatbots) and nine clinicians, using reflexive thematic analysis. Amid plentiful, often conflicting information, what participants most lacked was knowing when: whether a sensation was expected, how long post-exercise pain should last and when it signalled harm. AI tools answered at any hour and settled bounded questions. In participants’ accounts, tools restated known limits, hedged in the grey zone between discomfort and harm, addressed moments rather than the course of care, and reversed under challenge without reasons. Generic information could stop treatment; starting and sustaining it followed most readily when a source was person-specific, timed to their course and answerable. Patient-facing AI should elicit the course, convey clinician-set criteria, follow up, explain revisions, hand off to clinicians and be evaluated over time.

items.title: Whose Carbon Is It Anyway? Exploring Household Dynamics in Sustainable Mobility Tracking
items.abstract: Transport behaviors are a major contributor to carbon emissions, and decisions are often made at the household level around what form of transport to take and when. Technology, primarily eco-feedback interfaces (EFIs) have been suggested to support users in making environmentally friendly choices. However, there is a lack in understanding of how the underlying social dynamics of households influence decisions around sustainable practices, particularly through the lens of mobility. To understand how to design technology to better support households in negotiating around sustainable mobility choices, the research team interviewed 21 participants across nine households, probing them with four low-fidelity mockups representative of EFIs from prior work. We found that the varied mobility-related responsibilities among household members, as well as varying perspectives on the environment, can cause friction in the utility of EFIs in the home. We suggest that designs can account for these factors through acknowledging varied roles and perspectives.

items.title: Why We Say Yes When We Doubt: Trust, Social Pressure, and Independent Judgment as AI Changes Scams
items.abstract: Why can a request feel suspicious and still be difficult to refuse? Drawing on published research and my experience with Tech Talk for Seniors, this paper examines how emotion, social expectations, and the desire to help can lead people to comply despite their doubts. Artificial intelligence (AI) makes personally tailored messages easier to produce, increasing the importance of understanding what makes them persuasive. During short, high-pressure encounters, scammers can push people to act now, keep quiet, and check only through channels the scammer provides; I examine each as a point where that pressure might be resisted. A central insight is that people can step away and verify a request independently, even when they are unsure whether it is fraudulent. The paper connects this practical approach to a broader human question: how can support help people exercise their own judgment while preserving trust and independence?

items.title: A Didactic Analysis of the Design of Geometry Tasks Using Generative Artificial Intelligence by Prospective Primary School Teachers
items.abstract: Abstract This study analyses the didactic aspects prioritised by prospective primary school teachers when designing geometry tasks using generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). A qualitative and interpretative methodology was adopted, based on an intrinsic study of three case studies and a content analysis. Thirteen students on the Bachelor’s Degree Programme in Primary Education Teaching at a Spanish university took part, organised into three working groups. The data sources were their written reports and the conversations held with GenAI applications. A total of 158 text units were analysed using the components of the Didactic Suitability Criteria and six indicators of the quality of task instructions. The results reveal three key findings: first, the prospective teachers prioritised epistemic and cognitive aspects, particularly the richness of processes, the representativeness of mathematical objects, and high cognitive demand; second, they integrated interactional, mediational, and ecological aspects through cooperative work, autonomy, teacher mediation, manipulative and digital resources, and links to real-life situations; and third, GenAI helped to broaden ideas and refine activities but also produced responses that were overly formulaic, ambiguous, or didactically problematic. It is concluded that the integration of GenAI into initial teacher training requires didactic-mathematical knowledge, human supervision, and a critical evaluation of the proposals generated before their incorporation into school teaching.

items.title: A Dual-Loop Decision Support System for AIGC-Driven FMCG Print Advertisement Creative Generation
items.abstract: Creative decision-making under time pressure suffers from inefficient human–artificial intelligence (AI) collaboration and weak evaluation feedback. This paper proposes a dual-loop decision support system that integrates prompt diffusion, human-in-the-loop fine-tuning, and real-time multi-criteria scoring. Validated on print advertisement creatives from three fast-moving consumer goods brands using campaign logs, graphics processing unit records, and crowd ratings, the system achieves improved performance against end-to-end AI-generated content while maintaining creative diversity and brand alignment. Built-in feedback controls including anomaly rollback and version archiving optimize convergence processes and reduce computing resource consumption per project. The results confirm that structured human–AI iteration enhances both the speed and the quality of creative decisions, offering a robust, replicable decision support system architecture for intelligent content generation.

items.title: A Good-Practice Example for Teaching Generative Artificial Intelligence Competencies to (Future) Adult Educators
items.abstract: This article outlines the development and revision process of a good-practice example for a university seminar for adult education master’s students in Germany to teach Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) competencies. Through an examination of the discourse on the digital and GenAI divide, the necessary prerequisites for ac­quiring GenAI competencies are drawn upon and integrated into the seminar design. The article also traces how the module plan has evolved over the years based on evaluations and technological developments. Drawing on GenAI competency models and Freire’s pedagogy, the seminar’s primary aim is to provide students with a critical understanding of GenAI. Drawing on anonymous and personal feedback from students, the seminar has been refined continuously between 2023 and 2026, and is currently in its fifth iteration. Experience has shown that teaching a critical approach to GenAI is most effective through an examination format in which students create a future professional activity exclusively using GenAI.

items.title: A Socratically Scaffolded Personal AI Mentor for Postdigital Lifelong Learning
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are entering adult education without adequate andragogical grounding. This paper addresses that gap by developing an evidence-informed conceptual architecture for a Socratically scaffolded Personal AI Mentor in postdigital lifelong learning. The approach is conceptual framework development through theory-to-application translation, drawing on the author’s qualitative evidence synthesis (QES) of seven stud­ies of digital and e-mentoring in adult and professional learning. The theoretical base, grounded in Dewey’s pragmatism and transactional realism, integrates andragogy, transformative learning, critical inquiry, Socratic questioning, experiential learning, and social sustainability. The resulting architecture specifies six design compo­nents: goal-oriented engagement, a Socratic-Kolb inquiry process, a dialectic trace, resilient continuity, a human bridge, and agentic constraints. The paper concludes that AI mentoring should preserve learner agency, support reflective inquiry, sustain continuity, and connect learners to human communities.

items.title: A workflow-aligned framework for AI literacy in materials-informatics education: scientific judgment, equity, and curriculum design
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to predict materials properties, prioritize experiments, and generate hypotheses in materials science. The limiting challenge is no longer only algorithmic capability, but also whether students and educators can use AI with domain-specific scientific judgment. This conceptual analysis argues that AI education for AI-powered materials discovery should move beyond tool access and surface-level interaction with generative systems toward a workflow-aligned model of AI literacy. The analysis links AI literacy to core materials-informatics competencies: data provenance, domain-specific featurization, model validation, uncertainty quantification, physics-informed reasoning, reproducibility, and experimental feedback. It also advances an outcome-oriented equity perspective in which institutions evaluate not only access and participation, but also comparable learning gains, transfer of learning, learner confidence calibration, persistence, and research readiness across student subgroups. The article synthesizes relevant evidence, identifies cognitive and ethical risks such as off-loading and cognitive surrender, and proposes a dual-track curriculum model, implementation recommendations, reusable curriculum artifacts, and a set of testable propositions for future study. The central goal is to prepare students to become better scientists—not merely more efficient users of AI tools.

items.title: Affective and Functional Needs in AI Use: User Patterns and Their Relation to Real-Life Support and Well-Being
items.abstract: Conversational AI systems are increasingly used to fulfill both functional and affective needs, yet how users perceive the AI-adoption effects varies. Existing research tends to treat these two needs as binary categories and to classify users by a single dominant need. However, this approach fails to capture users who engage with AI for both affective and functional purposes simultaneously, leaving it unclear how these needs combine in real-world AI use. To capture the multifaceted nature of users' AI engagement, we developed the AI-Support measurement with 1,090 participants, grounded in social support theory, which evaluates four dimensions of perceived AI support: emotional/esteem, social companionship, informational, and instrumental support. This study provided (1) an AI-Support Scale developed to measure the perceived support types from human-AI interaction, (2) evidence that users might adopt AI with a high level of both functional and affective use, and (3) exploratory indicators of users' real-life social support and well-being, enabling descriptive results aligning with theoretical expectations. Overall, this study highlights the importance of understanding individual differences in AI affordance use, enabling AI systems to be designed in alignment with different user adoption profiles rather than assuming uniform benefits across all users.

items.title: AI and education in African national AI strategies: An analysis of 18 countries
items.abstract: Abstract National artificial intelligence strategies and policies assign education responsibilities both for developing AI capabilities (education for AI) and for adopting AI in educational services (AI for education). This study examines how these responsibilities are articulated and supported in a bounded corpus of 18 African national policy documents. A descriptive qualitative document analysis consolidated 275 evidence records, retaining source passages, locations, working translations, statement types and uncertainty notes. Document-level coding distinguished learning about AI, identifiable educational AI applications and educator preparation; a framework-based thematic synthesis examined delivery arrangements, inclusion and safeguards. Structured AI learning was identified in all 18 documents, named educational AI functions in 12 and educator preparation in 14. These counts include proposed and illustrative measures and do not indicate implementation; restricting them to proposed actions gives 17, 9 and 13. Educational applications ranged from personalised learning and tutoring to student profiling, admissions and credential verification. Supporting arrangements included teacher development, laboratories, scholarships, partnerships, institutional responsibilities and monitoring targets, but these elements were not interchangeable evidence of a complete delivery plan. Counter-examples to any general claim of weak specification included a costed education programme in Mozambique’s draft and proposed algorithmic bias audits covering education in Côte d’Ivoire. The corpus assigns education a dual role in AI development while specifying the connections between reforms, resources and protections unevenly. The contribution is an evidence-linked account of policy design, not a ranking of countries or an assessment of educational outcomes. Keywords: artificial intelligence; education policy; Africa; policy analysis; AI literacy; AI Strategy

items.title: AI as metacognitive mirror (AIM)
items.abstract: AI as Metacognitive Mirror (AIM) is a method for enhancing human metacognition through structured, AI-assisted analysis of observable behavior. AIM uses a decoupled architecture where the object behavioral data is analyzed in a separate AI session using an evidence-based codebook. AIM mirrors the identified cognitive patterns back to the user as metacognitive feedback. The method is non-directive, user-driven, and can be run with any sufficiently capable large language model. This project hosts the AIM method paper, the AIM meta prompt, and user manual. All materials are openly available under a CC BY 4.0 license for free use and further development. The prompt and codebooks will be updated here as the method evolves. See "Files" to find all the documents.

items.title: AI Awareness and Digital Innovativeness: The Mediating Role of AI Crafting and the Moderating Roles of Digital Leadership and AI Self-Efficacy
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly reshapes how organizations operate, innovate, and compete, employees face increasing pressure to adapt to rapidly evolving digital work environments. However, whether employees translate AI-related awareness into innovative outcomes may depend not only on their proactive adaptation behaviors but also on contextual and individual conditions. Drawing on the job demand-resource theory and social cognitive theory, this study develops and tests a moderated mediation model in which AI crafting mediates the relationship between AI awareness and digital innovativeness, whereas perceived digital leadership and AI self-efficacy serve as contextual and individual boundary conditions, respectively. Using single-wave, single-source data collected from 606 employees in China’s IT and manufacturing industries, the results indicate that AI awareness is positively associated with digital innovativeness through AI crafting. Moreover, perceived digital leadership and AI self-efficacy strengthen the positive associations between AI awareness and AI crafting and between AI awareness and digital innovativeness. These findings extend research on AI awareness by examining how employees’ awareness of AI-related changes is associated with digital innovativeness through proactive work adjustment and by highlighting the complementary roles of perceived contextual support and individual capability beliefs.

items.title: AI awareness relates to university students’ boundaryless career through the parallel mediation of intrinsic motivation and future job insecurity
items.abstract: The in-depth penetration of artificial intelligence (AI) technology has reshaped career forms and the structure of the labor market, exerting a profound impact on university students’ cognition and orientation towards career development. Based on the conservation of resources theory and self-determination theory, we conducted three studies—an experimental study and two survey studies—to explore correlational linkages between AI awareness and university students’ boundaryless career. Studies 1 and 3 consistently demonstrated that AI awareness is indirectly associated with boundaryless career through the parallel mediating pathways of intrinsic motivation and future job insecurity. Study 2 provided experimental evidence that heightened AI awareness increases both intrinsic motivation and future job insecurity. This research enriches the application scenarios of boundaryless career theory in the context of technological change, deepens the understanding of the mechanism linking technological perception to youth career psychology, and offers practical implications for career guidance in universities.

items.title: AI chatbots showed higher response accuracy than dentists, medical doctors, and the general public on radiation safety questions
items.abstract: Abstract Radiation is encountered in daily life through natural and artificial sources as well as in medical diagnostic and therapeutic applications, and its exposure may lead to adverse health effects. This study aimed to assess radiation-related knowledge among dentists, medical doctors, and the general public and to compare their response accuracy with that of AI-based chatbot systems. A 25-item multiple-choice questionnaire assessing radiation risks and radiation safety was administered to 344 individuals, including dentists, medical doctors, and members of the general public. The same questions were entered into seven selected AI-based chatbot systems (Claude, DeepSeek, Microsoft Copilot, Gemini, Perplexity AI, ChatGPT-5, and ChatGPT-4o). The response accuracy of the chatbots was compared with that of the human participants. In addition, the consistency of their performance across different users and time periods was comparatively analyzed. AI-based systems generally demonstrated higher accuracy rates compared to human participants. Accuracy rates ranged from 80 to 90.67% among AI-based systems, compared with 32–60% among human participants. Among the evaluated chatbot systems, Microsoft Copilot achieved the highest performance, while Perplexity AI exhibited the lowest. Among the human groups, dentists and medical doctors performed significantly better than the general public, with no significant difference between the two healthcare professional groups. Performance remained stable across morning, midday, and evening assessments for most AI systems; however, ChatGPT-5 showed a significant temporal difference ( p < 0.001). AI-based systems achieved higher response accuracy than human participants under the evaluation conditions used in this study. The overall performance of the human participant groups indicates room for improvement in radiation safety education. While AI-based tools may serve as valuable educational resources, their performance should not be interpreted as evidence of superior clinical judgment or decision-making ability.

items.title: AI DOES NOT JUDGE: EPISTEMIC ARCHAEOLOGY AND GOVERNANCE OF MEANING IN THE HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
items.abstract: The adoption of GenAI in research is reshaping the epistemic conditions of knowledge production. While LLMs are often perceived as neutral agents, this paper argues that the humanities and social sciences (HSS) serve as critical infrastructures for governing AI-mediated inquiry. Drawing on sociotechnical pragmatism, the article introduces epistemic archaeology: an interpretive orientation that treats AI outputs as stratified artifacts shaped by cultural and statistical histories. Rather than seeking validation in convergence, this approach interprets model divergence as signals of training data and epistemic constraints. By foregrounding interpretation, contextualization, and epistemic literacy, the work establishes the foundational coordinates for AI integration. This conceptual positioning preserves human responsibility and judgment as the primary locus of meaning in human–AI interaction. While serving as the theoretical base for future applications, the paper defines the ethical landscape for responsible academic research.

items.title: AI Implications for the Quality of Counselling Practice
items.abstract: Although the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming educational guidance and career counselling, its impact on quality and professionalism has not been sufficiently researched. This scoping review investigates how AI influences counselling methods and professional standards and analyses 20 publications (2015–2025) from two databases (ERIC and German Education Index) using a systematic micro-, meso-, and macro-level framework. Although research in this area has grown rapidly since 2022, concrete quality standards for AI-supported counsel­ling remain elusive. While AI can simulate empathy and provide reflective prompts, it cannot replicate genuine human warmth or address complex biographical issues. Acknowledging AI’s potential to enhance accessibility, it only serves as an expansion of the repertoire rather than a replacement for human reflexivity. In order to safeguard professional integrity in the postdigital era, the study recommends implementing mandatory AI competencies and establishing a digital commons infrastructure to protect counselling values from commercial interests.

items.title: AI IN THE INDIAN JUDICIARY: CAN TECHNOLOGY REDUCE PENDENCY WITHOUT REPLACING HUMAN JUDGMENT?
items.abstract: This article examines the potential of artificial intelligence to reduce judicial pendency in India without compromising human judgment. It explores existing applications, including SUPACE, SUVAS and eCourts Phase III, alongside judicial concerns regarding fabricated citations, algorithmic bias and automation bias. Through an analysis of relevant Indian judicial decisions, the article distinguishes AI-assisted research and administrative functions from adjudicatory decision-making. It argues that AI should complement, rather than replace, judicial reasoning through mandatory human verification, independent assessment of legal authorities and accountable use. The article concludes that responsible integration of AI can improve judicial efficiency while preserving fairness, accuracy and legitimacy.

items.title: AI Integration in Indonesian Education: Trends, Outcomes, and Challenges - A Comprehensive Review
items.abstract: Background Global education trends show the rapid growth of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as one of the leading technologies worldwide, a shift increasingly reflected in Indonesian education. This study aims to provide a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) by mapping the research landscape, its representation in practice and policy, its impact on learning quality, and the barriers to AI integration in Indonesian education. Method Using the PRISMA protocol, 34 peer-reviewed articles indexed in the Scopus and Google Schoolar databases (2020–2026) were systematically selected and thematically analyzed across four main themes. Results The findings indicate a rapid increase in publication productivity, particularly following the worldwide expansion of generative AI technologies after 2022. However, this growth remains unevenly distributed, concentrated in higher education institutions and urban centers on the island of Java, with a marked absence in primary and secondary education levels and in regions outside Java. The majority of AI-driven implementations consist of generative chatbots, adaptive learning platforms, and intelligent tutoring systems, alongside emerging applications such as learning analytics and AI-powered instructional media. Several studies included in this review reported that AI has contributed to measurable improvements in student outcomes including learning achievement, motivation, engagement, and teaching efficiency in well-implemented AI environments. Nonetheless, its adoption also poses significant risks, including a decline in students’ critical thinking skills, threats to academic integrity, and the absence of comprehensive data privacy policies and ethical standards governing AI use in education. Conclusion These findings underscore the urgent need for a responsible AI implementation framework in Indonesia one that incorporates standardized AI literacy competencies for teachers, locally contextualized ethical policies, and a functional national roadmap for AI-enabled educational transformation.

items.title: AI-Assisted Chinese-Western Cultural Comparison Course: A Conceptual Framework
items.abstract: This paper develops a framework for an AI-assisted Chinese-Western cultural comparison course by bringing together Byram’s intercultural communicative competence model, Vygotsky’s constructivism, and Huang et al.’s theory of cultural competence development. It identifies five interrelated course goals: cultural knowledge, cross-cultural practical ability, critical cultural awareness, AI collaboration literacy, and human-AI symbiosis awareness. To achieve these goals, three teaching strategies are proposed. First, content should be reconstructed through multimodal and professionally adapted resources; second, the learning process should be immersive and adaptive; third, assessment should be data-driven and multidimensional to evaluate the goals. The implementation conditions of these strategies are further discussed in terms of teacher AI competence, human-AI boundary negotiation, algorithmic bias mitigation, and differentiated task design. It provides a structured basis for AI-assisted Chinese-Western cultural comparison teaching and for future empirical testing of its effects.

items.title: AI-Augmented Behavioural Finance Pedagogy: Transforming Undergraduate and Postgraduate Classrooms through Simulation-Based Learning
items.abstract: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into higher education has transformed how business and management subjects are taught and learned. In finance education, traditional teaching methods often emphasize numerical calculations and theoretical frameworks while offering limited opportunities for experiential and behavioral learning. In this case study, the authors present a real classroom-based pedagogical intervention implemented in a course for undergraduate and postgraduate students at Commerce and Management Institutes in India, where AI tools and behavioral finance simulations through games were integrated into teaching practices to improve student engagement, analytical thinking, and practical decision-making skills. This case study emerged from observations by the teaching faculty who taught Behavioural Finance courses to undergraduate and graduate students, who frequently struggled to connect financial theories with real-world investment behaviour and market psychology. In an attempt to make students show their interest in learning this kind of course, which requires understanding the fundamentals of Psychology, which is a prerequisite for this course. To address these challenges, AI-assisted simulations, AI-generated market scenarios, interactive case discussions, and behavioural finance activities were introduced into the classroom in the form of a game. Students were exposed to emotionally driven financial decision-making situations, such as panic selling, herding behaviour, overconfidence bias, and speculative investment trends, through AI-generated business narratives and stock market simulations. The teaching faculty made an attempt through gamification as an intervention by adopting a simulation-based learning framework. Based on the authors' experience in teaching behavioural finance courses, a simulation was created using AI. This AI-generated investment simulation scenario was used as a pilot study in the real classroom. The students actively participated in games and were able to make decisions rather than absorb theoretical content. AI tools were used to generate realistic market situations, investment dilemmas, and personalised learning prompts that encouraged critical analysis and collaborative problem-solving. The results demonstrated and presented active classroom participation, improved conceptual understanding, enhanced critical thinking abilities, and greater student interest in finance subjects. Students reported that the integration of AI made finance learning more relatable, practical, and interactive. This case also discusses ethical concerns, faculty adaptation challenges, limitations of AI-generated learning environments, and recommendations for responsible AI integration in finance education. This case study contributes to the growing discourse on gamification through AI-enabled pedagogy by demonstrating how behavioural finance and AI can be combined to create immersive and mock experiential learning experiences in management education.

items.title: AI-Enabled Algorithmic Management and Frontline Employee Job Crafting: The Roles of Control, Support, and Managerial Orientation
items.abstract: Algorithmic management combines functions that regulate work with those that provide information and guidance, yet their distinct psychological and behavioral associations require further examination. Drawing on the Job Demands–Resources framework and a sociotechnical perspective, this study examines algorithmic control and support in relation to frontline employees’ job crafting, distinguishing system functions from perceived managerial enactment. Three-wave time-lagged survey data from 547 employees in fast-food chain outlets were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Algorithmic support was positively associated with work engagement and negatively associated with exhaustion, whereas algorithmic control showed the opposite pattern. Indirect-effect estimates were consistent with support being associated with greater promotion-focused crafting through engagement and lower prevention-focused crafting through exhaustion. Control was associated with greater prevention-focused crafting through exhaustion and lower promotion-focused crafting through engagement. The support–engagement relationship was stronger at higher perceived managerial decision-support orientation, while the control–exhaustion relationship was stronger at higher perceived enforcement orientation. These findings highlight the value of examining algorithmic functions across both motivational and strain-related pathways and considering how managers enact system outputs. The observational design supports associations consistent with the proposed mechanisms rather than causal conclusions.

items.title: Allocating cognitive work across people, language models and deterministic tools: A task-analytic method
items.abstract: Abstract People supervising language-model agents need to know what the agents decided and when to intervene. Reading every response becomes impractical as more work is delegated. We extend a task-analysis method to allocate decisions among deterministic tools, small language models, reasoning models and people, with each task represented as an observe, orient, decide and act cycle. Analysts specify its inputs, decision and output, and derive the information supervisors need from their goals. Allocation depends on how formally the decision can be specified, the cognitive control it demands, its Cynefin domain and whether it establishes facts or makes a normative choice. A machine tier withholds a decision when it declines, fails the output checks or falls below its confidence threshold. The decision then passes to the next tier. People retain normative choices and may store them as scoped policies. In a computational comparison with two open-weight models on 64 synthetic tanker-join instances, the allocated system was correct on 89.6% of required epistemic decisions, against 67.2% for a reasoning model given the whole task. It used about a third of the input tokens and an eighth of the output tokens. A scripted supervisor supplied 13% of its scored decisions. The small-model tier withheld 97% of its wrong candidates and the reasoning-model tier 93%, counting refusals, output checks and confidence thresholds together. The prototype failed to keep one training choice with people. Effects on supervisors' situation awareness and workload require a study with practitioners.

items.title: Anticipatory obsolescence and the aging workforce: A selection, optimization, and compensation perspective in the AI era
items.abstract: As workforce aging and artificial intelligence (AI) applications increasingly unfold in parallel, understanding how technological change reshapes older workers' adaptive processes and work attitudes has become critical. Drawing on selection, optimization, and compensation theory, this study introduces anticipatory obsolescence, the specific forward-looking perception of human capital depreciation that is distinct from general job insecurity, as a key conceptual lens for understanding the moderating role of AI-job substitution risk on the relationships between workplace opportunities and successful aging at work. Using data from 1449 workers aged 50 and over in the 9th wave of the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe , we examine the relationships linking workplace opportunities for new skills acquisition, job advancement, and job support with job satisfaction as a critical indicator of successful aging at work in the context of AI-related changes. Overall, all three types of opportunities are positively associated with job satisfaction. However, under high AI-job substitution risks, the effect of new skill acquisition is weakened, and the effect of job advancement is strengthened, while no significant moderation effect is observed for the relationship between job support and job satisfaction. This study contributes to scholarships by bridging macro-level objective indicators of AI-induced employment risks to micro-level subjective perception about future human capital value. We offer a nuanced understanding of change-related implications for the aging workforce and practical insights for supporting successful aging of the graying workforce.

items.title: Architecting agents for collaborative air combat using a team-centered design aproach
items.abstract: Abstract The United States Air Force seeks to develop “Collaborative Combat Aircraft” to provide an affordable force multiplier. Current Artificial Intelligence (AI) research efforts often focus on developing the AI necessary to support task work within target domains without sufficiently considering integration in existing systems, including the capabilities necessary to enable the teamwork required to enable human-AI teams. The current research employs a recently published team-oriented analysis and design method, referred to as Agent-Oriented Systems Modeling (AOSM), to provide an architecture-level analysis of the human-AI team to establish requirements for the AI systems in both manned and unmanned aircraft. The approach is applied to an F-16 formation performing defensive counter air, to evaluate task and teamwork requirements within the analogous system. These requirements, namely the goals, responsibilities, and capabilities of the agents in the existing system are then applied to envision the “To-Be” system to ensure equivalent or greater capabilities exist in the proposed architecture. This analysis produces numerous traceable findings that can be applied to establish system level requirements for future development to ensure effective human-AI teaming, including 45 capabilities required of the system and five agent roles to be fulfilled in the “To-Be” system. The project discusses and supports the importance of efficient communication and coordination mechanisms for all AI agents when teaming with the human pilot.

items.abstract: Transformations associated with digital culture and the expansion of Artificial Intelligence have intensified debates about the role of teachers and the nature of pedagogical decision-making. This article aims to propose and theoretically ground Learning Architecture as a theoretical-pedagogical perspective for understanding teaching practice, articulating intentionality, experience, interaction, meaning-making, and authorship. This qualitative, theoretical-conceptual, and interpretive study draws on research on learning, teacher agency, digital culture, and Artificial Intelligence in Education. Pedagogical decision-making is proposed as the transversal axis of the construct, guiding the organization of conditions for learning. The study concludes that technologies, methodologies, and AI systems do not occupy the center of the architecture, but function as resources subordinated to teachers’ educational purposes and pedagogical decisions.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Managerial Decision-Making: The Role of Human–AI Collaboration and Managerial AI Literacy
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being incorporated into organizational activities, including information processing, forecasting, customer management, resource allocation, and managerial decision-making. However, the organizational value of AI depends not only on technological adoption but also on how effectively managers collaborate with AI systems and understand their capabilities and limitations. This study examines the relationship between AI adoption and managerial decision-making, with particular attention to human–AI collaboration and managerial AI literacy. The proposed framework considers AI adoption as the independent variable, human–AI collaboration as a mediating mechanism, managerial AI literacy as a moderating variable, and managerial decision-making quality, decision-making speed, and organizational performance as outcome variables. A quantitative cross-sectional research design was adopted. Data were obtained from 200 respondents associated with the real-estate and construction ecosystem, including customers/property buyers, managers, engineers, architects, supervisors, labour personnel, brokers, investors, bankers, finance and accounting personnel, HR professionals, administrative staff, sales and marketing personnel, legal and compliance personnel, drivers, security personnel, cleaners, technicians, and other relevant stakeholders. Responses were measured using a five-point Likert scale. Based on the response distribution supplied for the present study, 180 respondents (90%) selected 5 (Strongly Agree) and 20 respondents (10%) selected 4 (Agree) for each reported questionnaire item. The resulting item-level mean was 4.90, indicating a strongly positive response pattern. The study provides a structured framework for examining how AI adoption, human–AI collaboration, and managerial AI literacy may jointly contribute to managerial decision-making and organizational performance. Respondent-level inferential analysis using PLS-SEM is required before reporting path coefficients, mediation, moderation, significance levels, and explained variance.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Related Considerations: Survey of Practicing School-Based Speech-Language Pathologists in Ohio
items.abstract: PURPOSE: Artificial intelligence (AI) is advancing rapidly with new tools and capabilities emerging quickly. Speech-language pathologists (SLPs) utilize AI in clinical practice, but it is unclear how SLPs use AI tools and the factors that SLPs consider in their decision making. This study presents a survey of school-based SLPs to (a) document the extent and nature of AI use; (b) assess the perceived quality and general opinions of AI; (c) identify ethical, legal, and institutional factors influencing their decisions; and (d) identify the types of AI training currently used and the training SLPs report wanting to receive. METHOD: Two hundred fourteen school-based SLPs across Ohio completed a survey about the types of AI tools they use, the factors influencing their use, general opinions about AI, and specific concerns about the use of AI in the workplace. The sample was predominantly White (91.3%) and female (97.1%). The average age was 45.17 years, with 19.72 years of professional experience. Participants who used AI within the last 6 months were categorized as "AI users" compared to "non-AI users" who had not. RESULTS: School-based SLPs reported using AI often in their practice across a wide range of tasks. SLPs reported concerns about accuracy or reliability, and ethical concerns as reasons for limiting or not using AI tools. Perceptions of AI quality were mixed, with SLPs divided on whether AI could produce outputs similar to an average practitioner. SLPs reported a significant need for guidance and training in AI tools and ethics. CONCLUSION: The results highlight the need for clear guidance on the use of AI tools, including ethical implications, along with additional training for school-based SLPs. items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Constitutional Rights in India: Regulating Algorithmic Decision-Making, Bias and Accountability
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into policing, welfare administration, employment, credit, education, healthcare, judicial and legal systems, and public administration. Algorithmic systems may improve efficiency, consistency and the processing of large quantities of information, but they may also reproduce or amplify discriminatory patterns embedded in historical data and institutional practices. Where governmental decisions affecting individuals are informed or generated by algorithms, constitutional concerns arise regarding equality, non-discrimination, privacy, dignity, autonomy, freedom, procedural fairness and access to remedies. India does not presently possess a single comprehensive AI-specific constitutional accountability framework. Nevertheless, Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution, together with administrative-law principles and the emerging data-protection and responsible-AI framework, provide a substantial foundation for regulating rights-affecting AI. This paper argues for a rights-based, risk-sensitive Indian framework incorporating algorithmic impact assessment, transparency, meaningful explanation, human oversight, independent auditing, institutional accountability and effective remedies.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Cybersecurity Support Tool for Nontechnical Users
items.abstract: This research examines the effectiveness of artificial intelligence as a cybersecurity support tool for nontechnical users. The study evaluated ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Claude 3 across five simulated cybersecurity scenarios involving phishing attempts, password reuse, fraudulent online stores, and suspicious security alerts. Using a standardized rubric, the study compared each model's threat recognition, safety recommendations, cybersecurity knowledge, clarity, and reliability. The findings highlight conversational AI's potential to improve cybersecurity awareness while also showing limitations in the accuracy, accessibility, and reliability of AI-generated security advice. The study emphasizes the importance of independent verification and human judgment when using AI to navigate online threats.

items.title: Artificial intelligence as a driver of organizational digitalization: Benefits, conditions and challenges
items.abstract: Abstract This theoretical article examines artificial intelligence in organizational digitalization. It distinguishes digitization, digitalization, and digital transformation, then combines sociotechnical theory with the dynamic capabilities perspective to explain how technology interacts with employees, routines, organizational structures and adaptation. The framework proposes that artificial intelligence supports transformation when aligned with strategy, integrated into processes and complemented by employee expertise, data and responsible governance. It highlights tensions involving discretion, bias, accountability and the fit between standardized systems and local practices. The article contributes propositions for empirical research and argues that AI’s value depends on integrating technical systems with human capabilities and organizational oversight. AI applications can automate repetitive tasks, analyze large amounts of data, personalize services and support decisions. However, their effects depend on data quality, employee skills, leadership commitment and the organizational context. For this reason, the article moves the focus beyond the simple adoption of AI and highlights the organizational capabilities and governance needed to integrate it responsibly. Keywords: artificial intelligence; organizational digitalization; digital transformation; dynamic capabilities; sociotechnical systems; AI adoption; responsible AI governance.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in archives: six modes of involvement and an ecosystem of trust — a reading in light of the theoretical-methodological framework of InterPARES
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) does not constitute a single phenomenon in archival practice. It may generate potential records, support archival functions, assist tool development, analyze holdings, become an object of preservation, or mediate access. Treating these different modes of involvement as homogeneous produces imprecise diagnoses and inadequate safeguards. This theoretical-conceptual article proposes a six-mode model: AI-assisted record production, AI tools for archival functions, AI-assisted tool development, AI analysis of archival holdings, AI systems as preservation objects, and AI-mediated access. Each mode is evaluated against common requirements of archival trust — authenticity, reliability, accuracy, and the chain of preservation — and is subject to a cross-cutting governance framework based on paradata, explainable AI, bias mitigation, ethical use, and accountable human oversight. The analysis is guided by the theoretical-methodological framework of InterPARES, particularly InterPARES Trust AI (2021–2026). The article concludes that AI can support archival work only when its use is governed by archival principles, documented procedures, and clearly assigned human and institutional responsibility. The model provides an instrument for analyzing AI initiatives, designing safeguards, and guiding future empirical validation through case studies.

This paper review s selected published research and international guidance to exam ine the potential benefits, m ajor risks, and future directions of AI in education. The literature indicates that AI can support personalized learning, provide tim ely feedback, assist educators w ith planning, and im prove access to learning support. A t the sam e tim e, its use raises concerns about privacy, bias, accuracy, unequal access, academ ic integrity, and over-reliance on autom ated system s. This paper uses a narrative literature-review approach rather than reporting a new experim ent or student survey. It concludes that AI should support— not replace— educators and learners, and that responsible adoption requires transparency, data protection, teacher preparation, hum an oversight, and evaluation in real educational settings.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education (AIHE): implications for personalized learning and institutional practices
items.abstract: Purpose This study addresses the following research question: What are the implications of artificial intelligence (AI) for Personalized Learning and Online Higher Education (OHE)? Design/methodology/approach A qualitative study was conducted using semi-structured interviews including faculty members and higher education administrators. The data were analyzed to identify the adoption factors, challenges, opportunities, and ethical considerations. An Integrative Model of Adopting AI in Online Higher Education (IMAOHE) was developed based on the empirical findings. Findings AI supports personalized learning through adaptive assessment, real-time feedback, learning analytics, and tailored content. The reported challenges include ethical dilemmas, institutional barriers, and the need to preserve teacher autonomy. Research limitations/implications Limited respondents and lack of student perspectives suggest future research with larger, more diverse samples and mixed-methods or longitudinal designs. Practical implications The model guides institutions, educators, and developers to integrate AI ethically and strategically, ensuring meaningful, context-aware learning. Social implications AI can enhance equity, inclusion, and student-centered learning while maintaining human mediation and cultural sensitivity. Originality/value This study provides an empirically grounded model linking AI adoption to pedagogical personalization in OHE, offering actionable insights for ethical and effective AI integration.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Mathematics Education: A Systematic Review and Evidence-Informed Framework for Productive Pedagogical Integration and Human–AI Interaction
items.abstract: This repository contains the supplementary data and materials supporting the systematic review entitled “Artificial Intelligence in Higher Mathematics Education: A Systematic Review and Evidence-Informed Framework for Productive Pedagogical Integration and Human–AI Interaction” by Felix O. Egara and Alfred M. Msomi. The review synthesises empirical research published between January 2021 and September 2026 on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher mathematics education. Searches were conducted in Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection, and 18 studies meeting the eligibility criteria were included in the review. The repository contains the original database search exports, the merged bibliographic dataset, the PRISMA 2020 reporting checklist, the full search strategies and eligibility criteria, the evidence-to-framework synthesis matrix, and the study characteristics and data-extraction matrix. These materials document the review’s information sources, study selection, data extraction, and evidence synthesis. They are intended to support transparency, methodological reporting, and further scholarly engagement with research on AI-supported mathematics learning in higher education.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Clinical Decision Support Systems for Emergency Department Triage and Acute Care Prioritization: A Systematic Review of Accuracy, Safety, and Implementation Readiness
items.abstract: Background:AI is being increasingly investigated as a clinical decision support tool for ED triage and acute-care prioritization. Machine-learning, deep-learning, natural language processing (NLP) and large language model systems have shown good predictive performance but concerns remain about under-triage, over-triage, generalizability, workflow integration and implementation safety. We systematically reviewed the accuracy, safety and implementation readiness of AI-driven clinical decision-support systems for ED triage.Methods:This review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 recommendations. PubMed/MEDLINE, PubMed Central, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science and Cochrane Library were searched (citation chaining, reference-list screening and recent systematic reviews were also used). Of the 1076 records identified, 312 duplicates were removed and 764 records screened; 79 full-text reports were assessed and 65 excluded; fourteen studies were included in narrative synthesis. Meta-analysis was not performed because populations, AI architectures, triage systems, reference standards and outcome metrics are highly heterogeneous.Results:Conventional machine learning, gradient boosting, neural networks, deep learning, natural language processing and large language models were included in the studies. AI systems generally outperformed conventional triage for critical illness prediction (hospitalization), intensive-care admission and mortality; reported AUROCs for early mortality were 0.962 and for 30-day mortality 0.925. Direct triage systems also had some success: KATE had 75.7% ESI assignment accuracy; prospective GPT-4 and GPT-4o studieshad κ = 0.899 and multicenter κ = 0.833 with F1 = 0.897 agreement with expert triage but safety outcomes under-triage/over-triage subgroup performance and patient-important outcomes were inconsistently reported.Conclusions:ED triage systems powered by AI have great potential as supervised clinical decision support tools but not yet enough evidence to justify autonomous deployment. Prospective multicenter validation, standardized safety metrics, subgroup analysis, workflow evaluation, governance and post-deployment monitoring are needed before widespread implementation

items.abstract: Description / Abstract Title: Safeguarding Trust in AI-Assisted Credit Scoring in Indian Digital Lending: A Documentary Analysis of the RBI’s 2025 Directions Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and alternative data increasingly inform digital credit decisions, raising critical questions about privacy, fairness, decision transparency, and accountability. In India, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued the Digital Lending Directions, 2025 on 8 May 2025. This study examines these Directions as a dated regulatory instrument and assesses their coverage of trust-related safeguards. Reviewing the 2025 framework alongside earlier Indian digital-lending instruments, the study applies a five-part analytical framework developed from the literature: decision transparency, privacy and data minimisation, fairness, human recourse, and model governance. It also compares the Indian framework with international guidance from the European Banking Authority (EBA, 2020), the OECD (2021), and the US NIST (2023). The documentary analysis reveals that while the RBI framework provides robust coverage of lender conduct, data consent, disclosures (such as the Key Facts Statement with all-in APR), and grievance redress, it exhibits notable gaps regarding mandatory pre-deployment fairness testing, ongoing model-drift monitoring, and standardised explanations for AI-assisted adverse decisions. To bridge these gaps, the study proposes a layered set of safeguards: privacy-by-design, standardised reason codes for adverse decisions, accessible routes to human review, and periodic fairness and drift audits.

items.title: Ask Before You Answer: A Question-Driven Evidence Reasoning Architecture (QERA) for In-Context Learning
items.abstract: AI assistants are increasingly asked to reason over a user's own web traces: group chats, community threads, activity logs and revision histories. On CL-bench Life, a benchmark of such real-life context learning, frontier LLMs solve fewer than one task in five. We find that the request is not the specification: over 80% of the benchmark's rubrics share less than 60% of their content words with the final request, as for a rule set two turns earlier or every record that meets the user's criterion, and LLMs answering directly pass only 67% of these implicit rubrics against 81% of the others. We propose QERA, a Question-driven Evidence Reasoning Architecture that asks before it answers. QERA first turns the request into a requirement checklist and typed information needs, filtered by code for faithfulness to the user's words; it then answers from the whole conversation, asks the same questions again with quotes verified by code, and applies a guarded local repair. It needs no training or rubrics and makes about four LLM calls per task. On all 405 tasks with four frontier LLMs, QERA attains the highest solving rate on every LLM (21.0% on average, against 18.2% for the strongest of three inference-time baselines and 14.6% for direct answering) and leads every baseline significantly when pooled across LLMs, while using fewer tokens than PSCI and 4-5% of the tokens of Ctx2Skill. Ablations on GPT-6-Luna show that the gain is settled before the answer, by a fixed answer protocol (+3.8 rubric points) and the request-specific questions (+1.6), and that it is concentrated on implicit rubrics, with checking afterwards refining mainly numeric requirements.

items.title: Assessing mentalization in humans and large language models
items.abstract: Abstract Mentalization - the ability to infer others’ beliefs and intentions to guide one’s own choices - is a key cognitive function underlying human social interactions. Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate behaviour consistent with humans on theory-of-mind tasks, yet whether these models can guide adaptive behaviour through mentalization is unknown. Here we use two economic games with cognitive computational modeling to uncover the latent strategies underlying mentalization in LLMs. We tested individual LLM agents across four model families, DeepSeek, GPT-4.1, GPT-5 and Gemini 2.0 Flash (N = 2,099), against opponents of varying sophistication and examined whether a prompting strategy designed to elicit strategic reasoning improved performance. We benchmarked results against human participants (N = 251) as a comparative measure. Across both games, LLMs showed clear behavioural and computational signatures of mentalizing that differed markedly by model provider and size. Strategic prompting generally improved performance by inducing more sophisticated reasoning, yet the extent of the benefit differed across the two tasks. Last, GPT-5 agents flexibly adapted their recursive depth of reasoning to increasingly sophisticated opponents, demonstrating superior performance to human participants. Collectively, we demonstrate different capacities for mentalization across LLMs, and highlight cognitive computational modeling as a formal method for assessing comparative intelligence across humans and machines.

items.title: Assistant or Ghostwriter? EAP Instructors’ Views on the Opportunities and Risks of GenAI in L2 Writing
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) systems are able to generate, revise and comment on second language (L2) student writing. However, less is known about where L2 writing teachers locate the opportunities and risks of such systems across the writing process. To that end, this study examined how English for academic purposes (EAP) writing instructors at two universities in Oman position GenAI within the L2 writing process. It focused on, first, the stages at which instructors locate GenAI's opportunities and risks, second, their views on GenAI as a source of feedback, and lastly their preparedness to manage academic integrity in AI-assisted L2 writing. A cross-sectional questionnaire combining Likert-scale items and open-ended prompts was completed by 51 EAP instructors , of whom 49 were retained for analysis. Closed items were analysed with descriptive statistics, Spearman correlations, McNemar tests and Mann–Whitney U tests. Open-ended responses were coded by writing stage through qualitative content analysis. The results showed that L2 writing instructors located GenAI's opportunities mainly in their own preparation of materials and model texts and in feedback. On the other hand, they highlighted its risks in students' drafting and in assessment. Revising and editing was contested, cited equally often as an opportunity and a risk. EAP instructors were more confident in using GenAI to prepare materials than in designing students' use of it at each writing stage. Just over half agreed that AI improves their feedback. This view was related to their overall attitude towards GenAI but not to their confidence as feedback providers. Most instructors felt responsible for checking students' GenAI use and confident in setting boundaries, but their confidence in maintaining academic integrity was unrelated to this sense of responsibility. More EAP instructors reported knowing how to use AI detectors than understanding how such detectors work. The study concludes that EAP instructors' readiness to integrate GenAI into L2 writing teaching and learning is uneven across the L2 writing process. Professional learning and development should therefore target the pedagogical design of student-facing AI use, the evaluation of AI feedback, AI detection literacy, and L2 writing assessment redesign.

items.title: Attitudes and perceptions toward the use of artificial intelligence chatbots for peer review in medical journals: a large-scale, international cross-sectional survey
items.abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence chatbots (AICs) are increasingly being considered for use in scholarly peer review to assist with tasks such as identifying methodological issues, verifying references, and improving language clarity. However, concerns remain regarding their reliability, ethical implications, and transparency. Evidence on how medical journal peer reviewers perceive the role and impact of AICs is limited. This study explored reviewers’ familiarity with AICs, perceived benefits and challenges, ethical concerns, and anticipated future roles in peer review. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional online survey of medical journal peer reviewers. Corresponding author information was extracted from MEDLINE-indexed articles added to PubMed within a six-week period. A total of 72,851 authors were invited via email to participate; those who self-identified as peer reviewers were eligible. The 29-item survey assessed familiarity with AICs and perceptions of their benefits and limitations in peer review. The survey was administered via SurveyMonkey from April 28 to June 16, 2025, with two reminder emails sent during the data collection period. Results Of 66,679 email invitations, a total of 1260 respondents provided survey responses (response rate: 1.9%), of whom 1157 met the eligibility criteria, and 1077 answered the main survey questions. Most participants were familiar with AICs (86.2%) and had used them for general purposes (87.7%), though most report not using AICs for peer review purposes (70.3%). Most respondents reported that their institutions do not provide training on AIC use in peer review (69.5%), although many expressed interest in such training (60.7%). Perceptions of AIC benefits were mixed, while concerns were widely shared, particularly regarding potential algorithmic bias (80.3%) and issues related to trust and user acceptance (73.3%). Conclusions While familiarity with AICs is high among medical journal peer reviewers, their reported use in peer review remains limited. There is clear interest in training and guidance, however, concerns related to ethics, data privacy, and research integrity persist and should be addressed before broader implementation.

items.title: Avoiding Cognitive Surrender in AI-Driven Ergonomics: A 27-Year Brazilian Perspective for the Global Market - From Reactive to Predictive
items.abstract: AbstractThis article explores the concept of Cognitive Surrender in AI-Driven Ergonomics — the risk that as AI becomes more competent in safety, human judgment is outsourced. Drawing on 27 years of EHS experience in Brazil (SP, GO, RJ, MS) managing Safety, Fire Protection and Road Safety in sugar-ethanol plants, soybean processing and construction, and now building EkoSeg EHS US LLC in Salt Lake City, UT, the author argues for AI for Augmentation, not Automation. The study bridges Brazil's NR-17 Ergonomic Work Analysis (AET) and OSHA's MSD prevention, analyzing the emergence of computer vision solutions like Kinebot (Curitiba), validated by Marfrig, P&G, Electrolux, with R$3M investment in Feb 2026 for global expansion. Kinebot delivers 5x faster and 80% cheaper analysis via phone video. The author presents lessons from the 62nd NISO Conference, Killarney, Ireland (2026): dashboards (Power BI integrating Safety Observations, NC, OFI, Near Miss, Training Expiry) don't save lives alone; conversations do. A framework is proposed: (a) Keep the Worker in the Loop — every AI high-risk flag (RULA 7) must trigger a Gemba walk, (b) Use Leading Indicators — % stations analyzed by AI, training validity, (c) Bridge NR-17 and OSHA. Author: Jailton da Silva, EHS Manager, 27 Years in HSE, Founder EkoSeg EHS US LLC & EkoSeg Segurança e Meio Ambiente, Brazil to Utah. items.title: Baby-schema-related cues shape moral expectations about decision-makers: evidence from names, faces, and AI avatars
items.abstract: People routinely form expectations about how others will behave in morally difficult situations, and such expectations guide consequential decisions, including whom to trust, hire, or delegate responsibility to. The present research examined whether baby-schema-related cues systematically bias these moral predictions. Across three experiments with Chinese university students (total N = 858), we tested three manifestations of baby-schema-related cues that share the function of evoking infant-like associations: repeated two-syllable names (Experiment 1), babyfaced appearance (Experiment 2), and visually cute artificial intelligence (AI) avatar designs (Experiment 3). Participants consistently perceived decision-makers displaying baby-schema-related cues as less likely to make utilitarian choices involving direct harm to others. The results show that superficially irrelevant social cues can bias moral expectations about others, although the underlying psychological mechanism remains to be clarified. These findings are relevant to moral psychology, person perception, and the design and evaluation of AI systems.

items.title: Babysitting AI Agents: A User-Centered Taxonomy and Study of Agentic Delegation Failures
items.abstract: Users are increasingly delegating tasks to AI agents, allowing agents to perform long-running, multi-step workflows on their behalf. However, agents may perform these tasks in ways that depart from users' expectations for how they should be carried out, leading to what we call agentic delegation failures. We leverage a large corpus of 163,487 Reddit posts, describing AI agent use, to develop MANDATE: a taxonomy of 23 failure categories organized into seven groups. A follow-up study with 73 AI agent users examined the relationship between prevalence and perceptions of severity and noticeability, finding that failures rated as more severe are considered harder to notice, and that prior experience with a failure is associated with greater noticeability. Finally, we assess the maturity of research on each failure and identify commonly encountered failures that have received little attention (e.g., agents running without making progress). Our findings inform opportunities to make delegation easier for users to oversee and better studied by the research community.

items.title: Balancing Innovation and Humanity: Advanced Practice Nurses Harnessing AI in Mental Health Care
items.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing mental health care through applications in screening, risk prediction, clinical decision support, documentation, and patient engagement. While these technologies improve efficiency and access, they also present ethical, clinical, and equity challenges that must be addressed in advanced practice nursing. This review synthesizes contemporary evidence on AI in mental health care and discusses its implications for advanced practice nurses (APNs), focusing on ethical implementation, equitable care, and policy. METHODS: An evidence-informed review of literature from 2019 to 2025 was conducted across various databases, including PubMed, CINAHL, and Google Scholar. The review covered AI applications, ethical considerations, health equity, and governance to identify themes relevant to APN practice. RESULTS: AI can enhance psychiatric assessments and patient engagement when used as a decision-support tool. However, challenges such as algorithmic bias, inconsistent performance, privacy concerns, and reliance on AI-generated recommendations persist. Emphasizing AI literacy, competency, and governance is crucial for safe, equitable implementation. CONCLUSION: APNs are well-suited to lead the ethical integration of AI in mental health care by merging evidence-based practice and patient advocacy. Ongoing investment in education, policy, and equitable governance is vital for maximizing AI's benefits while maintaining strong therapeutic relationships and quality care.

items.title: Barrier Verification and Leading-Indicator Governance for High-Risk Technical Operations in Oil and Gas and Construction Projects: An Integrative Review
items.abstract: High-risk technical operations in oil and gas facilities and construction projects remain difficult to control because work is temporary, interfaces are fragmented, hazardous energy is frequently introduced or released, and schedule pressure can weaken otherwise mature safety systems. This review examines how safety interventions can be configured so that engineered barriers, work-control verification, competence assurance, contractor governance and leading indicators operate as a connected assurance system rather than as isolated programs. A structured integrative review of peer-reviewed literature published from 2020 to 2025 was undertaken, with emphasis on construction safety, oil and gas safety climate, proactive indicators, digital work controls and sociotechnical risk management. The evidence shows that personal-safety programs are valuable for routine exposure reduction, but they do not by themselves provide credible assurance against low-frequency, high-consequence events. Stronger intervention logic emerges when the control selected is matched to the failure mode: physical barriers for hazardous energy, verified permits and isolations for temporary configuration change, competence controls for judgement-intensive tasks, disclosure mechanisms for weak signals, and governance controls for contractor and schedule interfaces. Leading indicators are most useful when they measure the condition of these controls rather than the volume of safety activity. The review develops an integrated assurance framework and proposes practical indicator families for project and operational settings. The central conclusion is that intervention quality depends less on the number of safety initiatives than on whether each critical control is owned, independently verifiable, time-sensitive and connected to decision authority before exposure escalates.

items.title: Barriers to Adopting AI-Driven Design Technologies in Architectural SMEs in Developing Countries: Evidence from a Delphi Survey in Iraq
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is entering architectural design through generative modelling and data-assisted decision support. In developing countries, most of this work is still carried out by architectural small and medium-sized enterprises with limited resources and uneven digital infrastructure. Existing studies have rarely examined how barriers to AI-driven design are ordered. This paper addresses that gap in Iraq. A literature list of 30 statements was refined by a 15-member Delphi panel into 22 barriers in five dimensions. The measurement model was assessed with partial least squares structural equation modelling on 83 practitioner responses. Interpretive structural modelling and MICMAC analysis then placed the dimensions in hierarchy, and the resulting paths were tested on the same data. Economic and institutional deficiencies occupy the driving level. Technological and data readiness acts as a linking layer, while human and organisational capacity and professional risk appear as dependent outcomes. All four paths were significant, the strongest running from institutional deficiencies to technological readiness. The findings indicate that economic and institutional conditions occupy the driving level in the expert hierarchy, while human capacity and professional risk appear as dependent outcomes. All four adjacent paths implied by that hierarchy were statistically significant in the survey data.

items.title: Being a role model for preventive action
items.abstract: This article highlights the crucial role of clinicians as role models in fostering preventive action within medical education. Role modeling is a powerful mechanism in workplace learning, contributing both to medical students' professional identity formation and to their self-efficacy through observational (vicarious) learning. Rather than learning from a single exemplary physician, medical students construct a “mosaic” of role models, drawing on diverse professionals who each demonstrate different competencies. This underscores the importance of exposing medical students to varied clinical perspectives. Despite the growing importance of prevention—driven by aging populations, increasing multimorbidity, and health inequities—medical students report limited exposure to role models who explicitly demonstrate preventive care. Preventive actions are often underrepresented or remain implicit in daily clinical practice, partly because curative care is prioritized and population-level activities are less visible. Additionally, clinicians may not recognize or articulate their own preventive efforts as role modeling opportunities. To address this gap, the article introduces a framework describing preventive action at both individual and population levels, structured around three steps: identification, intervention, and evaluation. Building on this, it outlines how clinicians can model preventive care effectively using four phases of role model learning: attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation. Practical strategies include making preventive actions visible, explaining underlying reasoning, creating opportunities for practice, and demonstrating outcomes. The article concludes that deliberate and explicit role modeling of prevention, combined with active student engagement, can strengthen learning and support the integration of preventive care as a core component of medical professionalism.

items.title: Belief-Conditioned Multi-Agent Actor Critic for Decentralized LLM Collaboration
items.abstract: Recent work has explored optimizing LLM collaboration through Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), but many approaches still rely on predefined workflows, limiting efficiency and scalability. Decentralized LLM collaboration is challenging because agents execute independently with limited communication, share a joint objective, and must infer useful information from communication traces. In this paper, we propose BCMAAC, a Belief-Conditioned Multi-Agent Actor-Critic method that maintains beliefs over contextual information and uses them to facilitate training. Experiments on Minecraft game-playing, web searching and tool-using tasks show that BCMAAC improves task performance and collaborative behavior compared to naive actor-critic baselines. The improvements are particularly pronounced in multi-turn tasks with richer contextual information, where belief modeling provides a clear advantage.

items.title: Beyond access: Engagement with conversational AI-assisted feedback shapes cognitive load in digital game-based learning
items.abstract: To examine the cognitive consequences of conversational AI-assisted feedback in complex digital learning environments, this study employed a between-subjects longitudinal field design to investigate how both access to and actual engagement with conversational AI-assisted feedback were associated with students' perceived extraneous and germane cognitive load during a five-week business simulation game. Because conversational AI-assisted feedback represents an interactive form of instructional support whose effectiveness depends on learner-related and contextual characteristics, the study further examined the moderating roles of simulation progression (time), intrinsic cognitive load, and metacognitive self-regulation. The findings indicate that regular engagement with conversational AI-assisted feedback did not uniformly reduce extraneous cognitive load; rather, its effects depended on learners' intrinsic cognitive load and the progression of the intervention. In contrast, students who regularly engaged with the conversational AI-assisted feedback reported significantly higher germane cognitive load than both students without access to the chatbot and students with access who did not use it. Overall, the findings advance understanding of human-AI interaction by demonstrating that the cognitive effects of conversational AI-assisted feedback are shaped by dynamic patterns of learner engagement, individual learning characteristics, and temporal changes during extended AI-supported learning interventions.
